# Regression and Multilevel Modeling

## Overview
This example uses data from a reaction time experiment where observers searched for a green circle amongst rectangles, and were asked to report if a line inside the green circle was vertical or horizontal. On some trials, a red rectangle was present, i.e, a distractor. The experiment was conducted in two ways: (1) a random ordering of distractor present and absent trials, and (2) a blocked ordering of distractor present and absent trials. With blocked administration, presumably participants had time to habituate to the distractor and would have a smaller response time decrement as compared with the random presentation condition. 

In this example analysis, we will first take a simple approach, and conduct a linear regression, on participant block-level means of response time. Thereafter we will apply multilevel modeling to better capture the nesting and variability inherent in the trial-level data.

The comparison illustrates a general principle: aggregation can simplify a question, but it can also discard trial-level information and obscure dependency among observations. Multilevel models represent repeated trials nested within participants directly.

## Load libs

The workflow uses tidyverse tools for preparation, `lme4` for mixed-effects models, and later helper packages for equations and publication-oriented summaries.

```r
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
```

## Load data

Always inspect raw dimensions, names, and representative rows before filtering. Reaction-time files often include practice trials, missing identifiers, incorrect responses, and timing outliers that require explicit decisions.
```r
exp_df <- read_csv("data/exp1.csv")
```

```r
# show data structure
head(exp_df)
```
---

## Pre-process data

Preprocessing defines the analytic sample. Here records without participant identifiers are excluded; a complete analysis should also document decisions about practice trials, accuracy, and implausibly fast or slow responses.
```r
# filter
exp_pp <- exp_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(PARTICIPANT))
```

### Create additional columns, remove columns

Renaming and reordering create a clearer analysis table. The binary presentation variable encodes blocked versus random administration, but its reference category should be recorded before interpreting a coefficient.
```r

exp_pp_ = exp_pp %>%
  mutate(is_practice = ifelse(practice == "yes", 1, 0)) %>%
  mutate(TRIAL = count_trial_sequence) %>%
  select(-count_trial_sequence, -response_time, -practice) %>%
  select(datetime, PARTICIPANT, BLOCK, TRIAL, is_practice, correct, RT, everything()) %>%
  mutate(EXP_BLOCK_RANDOM = ifelse(isRandom == "blocked", 0, 1))
```

---

### Get unique metadata

Participant- or session-level metadata should appear once per higher-level unit. Creating a distinct table makes duplicated or conflicting metadata easier to detect before joining.
```r
metadata = exp_pp_  %>%
  select(datetime, contains("DT_"), PARTICIPANT, contains("EXP_")) %>%
  distinct()
```

---

## Produce simple aggregates

Participant summaries provide a useful descriptive view and support the initial regression. Quantiles are included because reaction-time distributions are often skewed and may not be well described by the mean alone.

```r
# overall means and record count by participant
part_means = exp_pp_ %>%
  group_by(PARTICIPANT, datetime) %>%
  summarise(mean_rt = mean(RT, na.rm=T),
            sd_rt = sd(RT, na.rm=T),
            q10_rt = quantile(RT, probs=0.1, na.rm=T),
            q90_rt = quantile(RT, probs=0.9, na.rm=T),
            n_correct = sum(correct),
            n = n()) %>%
  inner_join(metadata)

# overall means by block
part_means_byblock = exp_pp_ %>%
  group_by(PARTICIPANT, datetime, BLOCK, is_practice, distractor) %>%
  summarise(mean_rt = mean(RT, na.rm=T),
            sd_rt = sd(RT, na.rm=T),
            q10_rt = quantile(RT, probs=0.1, na.rm=T),
            q90_rt = quantile(RT, probs=0.9, na.rm=T),
            n_correct = sum(correct),
            n = n()) %>%
  inner_join(metadata)
```
### Mean center the reaction times

Person-mean centering expresses each trial relative to that participant's typical response. Centering changes coefficient interpretation, so the chosen reference must be described whenever centered variables enter a model.
```r
exp_m = exp_pp_ %>%
  inner_join(part_means) %>%
  mutate(imean_c_RT = RT - mean_rt)
```
---

## Data visualization

Visualize distributions before modeling. The boxplots reveal differences in center, spread, and possible outliers across blocks and presentation conditions that a single coefficient could conceal.

```r
ggplot(part_means_byblock %>% filter(!is_practice), aes(BLOCK, mean_rt, group=BLOCK, color=as.factor(EXP_BLOCK_RANDOM))) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ EXP_BLOCK_RANDOM) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x= "Experiment Block", y = "Mean Response Time (ms)")
```

---

## Predictive Modeling

A model is a formal statement about an outcome, predictors, and error structure. Begin with the simplest model that answers the question, then add complexity for a substantive reason rather than only to improve fit.

## Run simple regression on block means

This regression treats block summaries as independent observations. It is easy to communicate, but repeated blocks from the same participant violate that independence assumption.
```r
fit = lm(mean_rt ~ n_correct + distractor, data=part_means_byblock)
summary(fit)
```

### Show resulting model equation
```r
# show model equation
library(equatiomatic)
extract_eq(fit, use_coefs=TRUE, wrap=TRUE)
```

## Run as series of incremental multilevel model

The incremental sequence starts with a random-intercept model and adds predictors one group at a time. The participant intercept captures stable differences in overall response speed while fixed effects describe average associations.
```r
# run models, starting with unconditional means model
fitm_0  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ 1 + (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
fitm_1  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ TRIAL + (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
fitm_2  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ TRIAL + is_practice + (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
fitm_3  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ TRIAL + is_practice + correct + (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
fitm_4  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ TRIAL + is_practice + correct +
                       distractor + 
                       (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
fitm_5  = lme4::lmer(RT ~ TRIAL + is_practice + correct +
                       distractor + 
                       display_size + 
                       EXP_BLOCK_RANDOM +
                       (1|PARTICIPANT),
                      data=exp_pp_)
```

```r
extract_eq(fitm_5, use_coefs=TRUE, wrap=TRUE)
```

### Compare models

Likelihood-ratio comparisons ask whether additional terms improve fit enough to justify added complexity. Nested model comparisons should be planned carefully and interpreted alongside effect sizes, uncertainty, diagnostics, and theory.
```r
# compare models
anova(fitm_0, fitm_1, fitm_2, fitm_3, fitm_4, fitm_5)
```

## Create publication-ready table of results

A formatted table helps readers inspect estimates and uncertainty, but formatting is not validation. Check convergence, residual patterns, influential cases, and the plausibility of the random-effects structure first.
```r
sjPlot::tab_model(fitm_0, fitm_5)
```

## Create publication-ready figure of results

Predicted-value plots translate coefficients back to the outcome scale. Include axis labels, units, uncertainty intervals, and a caption that identifies which variables are held constant.
```r
sjPlot::plot_model(fitm_5, type="pred")
```

## Takeaways

Choose the level of analysis to match the data-generating structure. Aggregated regression is useful for orientation, while multilevel modeling preserves trial-level variation and participant clustering. In either case, preprocessing decisions and diagnostics are part of the result—not optional steps hidden behind the final table.
